newsitem.title: BELARUS: Russia, Belarus mark withdrawal of Soviet missiles.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Belarus mark withdrawal of Soviet missiles.

text.p: Belarus and Russia, in a show of brotherly Slavic unity, marked the withdrawal of the last Soviet nuclear missile on Wednesday and reiterated strong opposition to NATO expansion eastwards.

Moscow sent its defence minister to the ceremony at a village west of Minsk, proving President Alexander Lukashenko could count on his eastern neighbour as the West slammed him for assuming sweeping powers.
Lukashenko himself was in Minsk, pushing through plans to restructure rival institutions and extend his term beyond 2000 after winning a plebiscite from voters on Sunday.

He sent acting Defence Minister Alexander Chumakov and the secretary of his Security Council, Viktor Shayman, to meet Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and the commander of Russian rocket forces, Igor Sergeyev.
The last missile rolled slowly into the last carriage of a train already laden with six disarmed SS-25s which then left for Russia, now home to the entire former Soviet arsenal.
"We are moving away missiles but NATO may already be planning to expand its arsenal, including the nuclear one, closer to the territory of Belarus and Russia," Rodionov said.

"Some Western politicians and strategicians are forcing through NATO expansion, supposedly to increase security. I ask, security from whom?" he said, adding: "We are resolutely, definitely against NATO expansion eastwards."

The ceremony at the military base 220 km (140 miles) west of the capital marked the final withdrawal of nuclear weapons on former Soviet territory to Russia, which had to take place this year in line with the START-1 arms reduction treaty.
Lukashenko had threatened to keep the last of 72 missiles as a bargaining chip against the Western alliance's plans to allow central and eastern European states join their ranks.
"A new non-nuclear state has appeared on the world map," Rodionov said, before the missiles departed to the strains of a military march called "Farewell to the Slav woman."

"From today Belarus obtains the status of a non-nuclear state and has fulfilled its international obligations," said Chumakov, who has taken over the defence ministry from Leonid Maltsev, sacked by the president this month for turning up drunk at an official event.
Shayman demanded that the West return the favour by guaranteeing it would not place nuclear arms on the territory of eastern countries who are seeking NATO membership.
"Belarus has liberated itself of nuclear weapons, despite the forecasts of some sceptics and experts. We have the right to count on analogous steps from European states," he said.
But he added that security in Belarus would be guaranteed by its membership of a community with Russia agreed this year and the Commonwealth of Independent States' security structure.
Officers and soldiers of the Russian missile forces' 49th division looked on as the four men spoke from a red platform with a slogan reading "Slav peoples' friendship forever."
The actual warheads from the missiles had already left, the final one two days before Lukashenko's referendum, which threw the former Soviet republic of 10 million into political crisis.
Belarus, bordering Russia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Ukraine, was the only former Soviet state outside Russia which still had nuclear missiles on its soil.
All the warheads were under Russian control and they could not be launched without Moscow's command.

Lukashenko, who switched the ceremony from Tuesday, said he wanted U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry to attend as well, but Washington has shunned him since he ignored its pleas not to go ahead with the referendum.
